title: TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner
articleTitle: The Evolution of Supply Cost Eligibility in Research and Development Tax Credit Jurisprudence: An Analytical Study of TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner and Its Legislative Progeny
subject: Qualified Supplies
summary: TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), is a U.S. Tax Court ruling on the federal R&D tax credit under I.R.C. §§ 41 and 174. It holds that depreciable character is measured in the hands of the taxpayer, so production molds a manufacturer sells to customers can qualify as supply qualified research expenses, even if retained on-site.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

In TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009) (133 T.C. No. 13, Docket No. 8333-06, filed November 12, 2009), the United States Tax Court issued a landmark precedential opinion defining the statutory boundaries between eligible "supplies" used in the conduct of qualified research and excluded "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) §§ 41 and 174. Decided on a fully stipulated record pursuant to Tax Court Rule 122, the ruling resolved a dispute between TG Missouri and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) over the taxpayer's 1997–1999 research credits—rejecting a longstanding IRS position that treated most tangible property as depreciable—regarding whether production molds built by third-party toolmakers to the taxpayer's design specifications and subsequently sold to customers can qualify as supply Qualified Research Expenses (QREs).
Factual Background and the Taxpayer's Claim

The petitioner, TG Missouri Corporation (formerly known as TG (U.S.A.) Corporation), operated as a Missouri-based manufacturer of injection-molded products—such as steering wheels, air bags, and body side molding—for customers in the automotive industry. To manufacture custom injection-molded automotive parts, TG Missouri designed, developed, and utilized complex production molds. TG Missouri's engineering and commercial workflow ordinarily commenced when it received a Request for Quote (RFQ) from an automotive customer. The customer's RFQ included general product specifications and requirements and required TG Missouri to develop a basic technical design for the injection-molded product. After receiving the RFQ, TG Missouri contracted with the customer to develop a production mold that would enable TG Missouri to manufacture the desired product; under the contract, TG Missouri was entitled to payment only if it successfully designed and built a mold capable of producing a sample product and the customer accepted the products produced using the mold.

To execute the mold development contract, TG Missouri performed engineering design work and then either constructed the physical mold in-house or subcontracted the physical fabrication of the mold to a third-party toolmaker. When TG Missouri contracted with a third-party toolmaker, the toolmaker constructed the mold according to TG Missouri's design specifications and did not guarantee that the mold would perform to the customer's specifications or produce the desired part. TG Missouri first worked with the toolmaker to build a prototype mold used for a limited number of test runs to isolate design flaws, then engaged the toolmaker to build the production mold, accumulating the construction costs in a tooling inventory account. After the toolmaker finished construction, TG Missouri purchased the production mold—which was not yet capable of producing sample products to the customer's specifications—and incurred additional design and engineering costs (primarily engineer wages) to modify it, a process that generally took 24 to 36 months from RFQ to customer acceptance. Depending on the contract terms, the customer either purchased the completed mold, with title shifting to the customer once construction was completed and the customer paid for it, or had TG Missouri retain ownership of the mold. Crucially, although TG Missouri sold the production molds and transferred legal ownership to its customers, the customers left the molds in TG Missouri's physical possession at its manufacturing facility so TG Missouri could use the molds to produce commercial quantities of injection-molded automotive parts for those customers, while the customers retained the risk of loss for the molds.

On its federal corporate income tax returns for tax years 1997, 1998, and 1999, TG Missouri claimed the Research and Experimentation (R&E) tax credit under I.R.C. § 41. In calculating its credit, TG Missouri included the amounts paid to third-party toolmakers for the production molds that were sold to its customers as qualified "supplies" expenses under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). Following an examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue issued a notice of deficiency for tax years 1998 and 1999 (adjusting credits generated and carried across 1997, 1998, and 1999), disallowing the portion of TG Missouri's claimed research tax credits attributable to the third-party production mold costs.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

After TG Missouri conceded all other adjustments, the case was submitted fully stipulated under Tax Court Rule 122 on a single issue, and the Commissioner did not challenge the engineer wages claimed as QREs; the opinion therefore did not address whether TG Missouri's underlying engineering and mold development activities met the four-part definition of "qualified research" under I.R.C. § 41(d). Instead, the IRS mounted a strictly statutory challenge to the eligibility of the mold expenditures as "supplies" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and (C)(ii), read in conjunction with I.R.C. § 174(c).

The Commissioner contended that the production molds were subject to wear and tear, exhaustion, or obsolescence, had a useful life exceeding one year (as the parties stipulated), and were used in TG Missouri's trade or business to manufacture its customers' automotive parts, pointing out that TG Missouri depreciated the molds it retained and used them in the same manner as the molds it sold. Under the IRS's legal theory, the statutory exclusion in I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) for "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" established a generic, objective test based on the inherent physical nature of the asset in the abstract. Relying on I.R.C. § 167(a) and Simon v. Commissioner, 103 T.C. 247 (1994), and asserting that a taxpayer-specific reading would render the words "of a character" superfluous, the Commissioner argued that the molds possessed the intrinsic "character" of depreciable property regardless of whether TG Missouri or its customer held legal title and claimed the depreciation deductions.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The Tax Court evaluated the dispute through the interconnected provisions of I.R.C. §§ 38, 41, 167, and 174. I.R.C. § 38 allows a general business credit encompassing the research credit determined under I.R.C. § 41(a). Under I.R.C. § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer may claim a credit equal to 20 percent of the amount by which its qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year exceed its statutory base amount. Under I.R.C. § 41(b)(1)(A) and (b)(2)(A)(ii), QREs include in-house research expenses paid or incurred for "supplies used in the conduct of qualified research". I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C) defines the term "supplies" as "any tangible property other than—(i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation". Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) reiterates that supplies used in the conduct of qualified research cannot be property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation.

Furthermore, under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), research constitutes "qualified research" only if expenditures with respect to such research may be treated as expenses under I.R.C. § 174. While I.R.C. § 174(a) and (b) authorize the deduction or amortization of research and experimental expenditures, I.R.C. § 174(c) explicitly disallows deductions for expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of land, or for the acquisition or improvement of property to be used in connection with the research or experimentation and of a character which is subject to the allowance under I.R.C. § 167 (relating to allowance for depreciation) or I.R.C. § 611 (relating to allowance for depletion), specifying instead that only the annual depreciation or depletion allowances under §§ 167 or 611 may be considered as § 174 expenditures. Under I.R.C. § 167(a) and the regulations thereunder, an allowance for depreciation is permitted only for property used in the taxpayer's trade or business or held for the production of income where the taxpayer holds a capital investment and bears the economic loss from exhaustion, wear, and tear; depreciation is expressly disallowed for inventory or stock in trade held primarily for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business.
The Court's Final Holding and Regulatory Aftermath

The United States Tax Court rejected the Commissioner's generic "inherent physical character" argument and held in favor of TG Missouri. Analyzing the text and structure of I.R.C. §§ 167, 174(b), 174(c), and 41(b)(2)(C)(ii)—and comparing other Code provisions that use the same phrase, notably I.R.C. §§ 1239(a) and 453(f)(7), which expressly look to whether property is depreciable "in the hands of the transferee"—the Court ruled that the phrase "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" must be evaluated in the hands of the taxpayer claiming the credit, rather than through a hypothetical or abstract assessment of the property's physical durability.

The Court emphasized that I.R.C. §§ 174(b), 174(c), and 41(b)(2)(C) must be read as a coherent scheme that prevents a taxpayer from expensing, or claiming a research credit for, the cost of property that is properly chargeable to a depreciable asset account on its books and more appropriately recovered over time through §§ 167 and 168 depreciation deductions. Because whether a taxpayer may depreciate property is a question of fact, the Court held that the phrase cannot refer to a generic depreciable character that exists without reference to a particular taxpayer and that taxpayer's use of the property. Because generally only a taxpayer with an economic interest in an asset—one who would suffer an economic loss from its deterioration and exhaustion—may depreciate it, and TG Missouri had sold the molds, TG Missouri held no such economic interest in those molds and could not claim depreciation allowances on them under § 167. Even though TG Missouri retained physical possession of the molds and used them to manufacture parts for its customers, the record did not show that TG Missouri suffered the economic loss from their deterioration: the customers bore the risk of loss, and TG Missouri adjusted its per-unit part pricing depending on whether it retained ownership (customers effectively paid a higher per-unit price when TG Missouri kept the mold). Consequently, the production molds sold to customers were not "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" in the hands of TG Missouri, the component-materials limitation of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4) (as then in effect) did not apply, and the amounts paid to third-party toolmakers were properly included as the cost of supplies in calculating the research credit under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).

The holding in TG Missouri reshaped federal R&D tax credit jurisprudence, and its conclusion was later reinforced by the Treasury Department's promulgation of final regulations under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 (T.D. 9680, July 21, 2014). Those regulations formally defined a "pilot model" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product, including a fully functional representation or model of the product, and clarified under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) that the ultimate success, failure, sale, or use of the product is not relevant to a determination of eligibility under § 174. Moreover, the final regulations include examples with fact patterns comparable to TG Missouri (such as the pilot models produced for sale in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(11), Examples 3 and 7), but they do not codify its facts: Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(5), Example 1, involves a tool manufacturer that orders a specially built machine from a third-party vendor—upon its order, at its risk, and without a guarantee of economic utility—to produce the manufacturer's own new tool, and confirms that only the vendor's engineering and design labor and the materials and supplies used to develop the appropriate design qualify, while the vendor's machine production materials and labor do not qualify under § 174.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

While TG Missouri resulted in a decisive statutory victory for the taxpayer on the stipulated issue, the litigation itself—and the wave of subsequent Tax Court and federal appellate decisions interpreting TG Missouri—exposes severe legal, accounting, contractual, and evidentiary vulnerabilities that routinely trigger IRS audit disallowances. A granular examination of the ruling and its doctrinal progeny reveals five core failure modes that determine whether tooling, prototype, and custom fabrication claims survive judicial scrutiny.
Fixed-Asset Capitalization and Retention of Depreciable Ownership (I.R.C. Sections 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and 174(c))

The primary catalyst for the audit dispute in TG Missouri was the bifurcation of tooling ownership and the accounting treatment applied on TG Missouri's 1997, 1998, and 1999 corporate income tax returns. In the manufacturing sector, suppliers frequently fabricate two distinct categories of experimental tooling: proprietary or self-retained tooling where the supplier retains legal title and amortizes or depreciates the asset over commercial part production runs, and customer-owned tooling where legal title transfers to the OEM upon tooling validation.

On its 1998 and 1999 returns, TG Missouri capitalized and depreciated the third-party toolmaker costs for the production molds it retained, claimed no research expenses or credit for those molds, and included as qualified research expenses only the toolmaker costs for the molds sold to customers; the IRS disallowed those latter amounts on the theory that the sold molds were nonetheless property of a depreciable character. Under the legal rule established by the Tax Court, because depreciable character is measured strictly in the hands of the taxpayer, any production mold, die, fixture, or prototype over which the taxpayer retains ownership and places into service as a commercial production asset is disqualifying "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" under I.R.C. §§ 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and 174(c). Taxpayers commit a fatal legal and accounting error when they either fail to execute a legally binding transfer of title for the experimental tooling to the customer—leaving the asset depreciable in the taxpayer's hands under § 167—or erroneously capitalize customer-sold tooling onto their own fixed-asset tax depreciation schedules and claim § 167 depreciation deductions rather than accounting for the tooling in non-depreciable work-in-process (WIP) or billable customer tooling accounts.
Mischaracterization of Third-Party Toolmaker Fabrication Versus Contract Research and the "Order and Risk" Requirement

A subtle but critical legal threshold in TG Missouri—one the Court did not itself address, because its holding rested solely on the depreciable-character issue—involves why payments made to third-party toolmakers to construct entire production molds could be claimed at 100 percent as in-house "supplies" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), rather than being restricted to 65 percent as "contract research expenses" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(3) or disallowed entirely under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3), expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of property that is not made "upon the taxpayer's order and at its risk" fail to qualify under § 174 if the property is otherwise depreciable, and under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2), payments to a third party that are contingent on the technical success of the third party's work are treated as the non-qualifying purchase of a finished product or result rather than qualified research.

In TG Missouri, the stipulated facts showed that the toolmaker built the molds according to TG Missouri's design specifications, that the toolmaker did not guarantee that the molds would perform to the customer's specifications or produce the desired part, and that TG Missouri was entitled to payment from its customer only if it successfully designed and built a mold capable of producing an acceptable sample product; although these facts are consistent with the order-and-risk principle later illustrated in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(5), Example 1, the Court allowed the toolmaker costs as supplies solely because the sold molds were not depreciable in TG Missouri's hands, and it did not rule on Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3), contract research treatment, or whether the costs were incurred to resolve technological uncertainty. Taxpayers fail this requirement when their procurement contracts delegate the engineering design and technical risk to the third-party toolmaker under a turnkey performance guarantee. If the third-party toolmaker guarantees that the mold will produce parts within tolerance before the taxpayer is obligated to pay the toolmaker, the expenditure is neither made at the taxpayer's risk under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3) nor eligible as contract research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2); instead, it is disqualified as the mere acquisition of a commercial asset.
Failure to Prove Investigative Intent and Disqualification of Commercial Inventory Supplies

Because the only issue remaining after concessions in TG Missouri was the depreciable character of the sold molds, the Tax Court did not have to adjudicate whether TG Missouri's molds were used for an investigative purpose. However, in subsequent litigation, the IRS aggressively attacked supply claims by citing Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012). In Union Carbide, a chemical manufacturer conducted process-improvement experiments on commercial reactors while continuing to produce chemical products for commercial sale. The taxpayer claimed the raw materials fed into the reactors during the test runs as supply QREs under § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). The Tax Court and the Second Circuit disallowed 100 percent of the supply costs, holding that because the raw materials had previously been held as standard inventory, would have been purchased regardless of whether any process research occurred, and were converted into finished goods sold in the ordinary course of business, the supplies were "at best, indirect research expenditures" incurred for the primary purpose of commercial production rather than research.

As the Tax Court subsequently clarified in Stephens v. Commissioner (Order denying partial summary judgment, Docket No. 11019-19, 2022), TG Missouri and Union Carbide establish a rigid evidentiary boundary. Under TG Missouri and Stephens, supplies purchased specifically to construct a custom product or pilot model for resale to a customer are not barred by the depreciable property exclusion merely because the asset is durable (the TG Missouri holding) and can qualify as supply QREs—even when built to fulfill a contractual obligation—provided the taxpayer proves that the physical unit was constructed for an investigative nature to test concepts and resolve design uncertainty. Conversely, if a taxpayer pulls standard raw materials from general commercial inventory that would have been purchased regardless of the research project, or claims raw materials used in routine commercial production runs after the mold design uncertainty has been resolved in violation of the I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) exclusion for research after commercial production, the claim fails under Union Carbide.
Failure to Satisfy the "Substantially All" (80%) Process of Experimentation Test and Lack of "Shrink-Back" Documentation

When taxpayers rely on TG Missouri and Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010), aff'd, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014), to claim the full fabrication cost of a first-in-class custom deliverable or tool as a "pilot model" supply QRE, they face the all-or-nothing cliff of the "substantially all" rule. Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), "substantially all" of the activities of the research must constitute elements of a process of experimentation related to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. The regulations define "substantially all" quantitatively, mandating that at least 80 percent of a business component's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, must constitute elements of a process of experimentation. If a custom machine, vessel, or tooling assembly as a whole fails the 80 percent threshold because more than 20 percent of its design and fabrication involves standard, non-experimental components or routine engineering adaptation—as occurred in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113—the entire parent business component is disqualified.

To salvage the credit when a parent pilot model fails the 80 percent test, the taxpayer must invoke the "shrink-back" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), stepping down from the overall product or mold assembly to the discrete sub-component or sub-assembly (such as a novel hot-runner manifold, conformal cooling insert, or specialized airflow core) that independently satisfies the four-part test. In Trinity Industries, Little Sandy Coal, and Betz, taxpayers suffered massive disallowances because their accounting and time-tracking systems tracked costs only at the macro contract or vessel level, leaving the court with no contemporaneous evidentiary basis to "shrink back" and isolate the supply and labor costs of the experimental sub-components.
The Funded Research Exclusion Cliff in Customer-Sold Tooling Contracts

Perhaps the most acute structural paradox created by TG Missouri is the tension between the depreciable property exclusion under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and the funded research exclusion under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H). To avoid the depreciable property exclusion under TG Missouri, the asset must not be depreciable in the taxpayer's hands—a result that followed in TG Missouri because TG Missouri sold the molds and its customers bore the risk of loss, leaving TG Missouri with no economic interest in them. The funded research exclusion was not at issue in TG Missouri, where the stipulated contracts entitled TG Missouri to payment only if it successfully designed and built a mold whose sample products the customer accepted. Yet the very act of contracting with a customer to develop and sell a custom mold for compensation triggers an immediate IRS challenge that the research is "funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) and controlling judicial precedents—including Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 405-17 (T.C. Dec. 6, 2019), Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), and System Technologies Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21 (T.C. 2024)—research performed under a customer contract is excluded as "funded" unless the taxpayer satisfies a strict two-prong test. First, with respect to economic risk and payment contingency, payment to the taxpayer under the contract must be contingent upon the technical success of the research, such that the taxpayer bears the financial risk of failure if the developed mold or pilot model fails to meet technical acceptance criteria. Second, the taxpayer must retain "substantial rights" in the results of the research. While transferring title to the single production mold to the customer was the fact pattern that defeated the depreciable property exclusion in TG Missouri and does not by itself strip substantial rights, if the customer contract also vests exclusive ownership of all underlying engineering designs, CAD models, tooling inventions, and manufacturing know-how in the customer and prohibits the taxpayer from reusing that technology without customer permission or royalty payments (as occurred in Tangel), the taxpayer retains no more than incidental benefits and loses 100 percent of the credit.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement implicated by TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner and its related case law against common taxpayer and IRS failures and the controlling judicial standard of proof.

Controlling Judicial Standard of Proof & Legal Rule

cells: IRS Error in TG Missouri: Asserted a generic "inherent physical character" test, arguing durable molds are per se depreciable property regardless of ownership. Taxpayer Failure: Retaining legal title to tooling used in commercial production, or capitalizing and depreciating customer-billed tooling on the taxpayer's fixed-asset tax ledger.

Taxpayer-Specific ("In the Hands of the Taxpayer") Standard: Depreciability is measured strictly in the hands of the taxpayer claiming the credit. If the taxpayer sells legal title of the mold to the customer and holds no depreciable economic interest under § 167, the mold is not depreciable in the taxpayer's hands (in TG Missouri, the customers bore the risk of loss and paid for the mold directly rather than through higher per-unit part prices) and qualifies as a non-depreciable supply even if physically retained by the taxpayer to make parts.
2. Third-Party Fabrication at Taxpayer's Order and Risk

Taxpayer Failure: Issuing turnkey purchase orders to third-party toolmakers where the vendor performs the engineering design and guarantees tool performance prior to payment, or misclassifying vendor-designed research as 100% supplies instead of 65% contract research.

Design Control & Risk-Allocation Standard: To claim 100% of third-party fabrication costs as supplies under TG Missouri (which decided only the depreciable-character issue, on stipulated facts showing that the toolmaker built to the taxpayer's design without a performance guarantee), the taxpayer should establish, consistent with Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3) and (b)(5) Ex. 1 (which, under current regulations, limit qualifying amounts to design and experimentation costs rather than post-uncertainty production costs), that it developed the uncertain engineering design in-house, ordered the third party merely to fabricate the physical component to those specifications, and bore the financial loss if the design failed.

IRS Argument: Contends that custom items built to fulfill a customer contract are commercial production goods rather than investigative models. Taxpayer Failure: Claiming standard inventory raw materials that would have been purchased regardless of research (Union Carbide) or claiming production run materials after design uncertainty is resolved.

Investigative Nature & Uncertainty Resolution Standard: A contractual obligation to build and sell a product does not preclude it from qualifying as a pilot model or supply QRE (TG Missouri; Stephens). The taxpayer must prove the physical unit was constructed specifically to evaluate and resolve technological uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design, and not pulled from routine commercial COGS inventory.

Taxpayer Failure: Relying on routine engineering calculations, standard vendor component selection, or customer-driven cosmetic/dimensional adaptations where the method and appropriate design are already established in the industry (Phoenix Design Group).

Objective Information Availability Standard: The taxpayer must demonstrate via contemporaneous engineering records that information available to it at the outset of the project could not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component without scientific or engineering experimentation.
I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), (d)(2); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5), (a)(6), (b)(2); Trinity Indus.; Little Sandy Coal

Taxpayer Failure: Claiming 100% of the material cost of a complex deliverable where >20% of the assembly comprises commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) or non-experimental components, while failing to maintain sub-assembly cost accounting to support "shrink-back".

Systematic Evaluation & Quantitative 80% / Sub-Component Standard: The taxpayer must prove a structured process of evaluating alternatives (modeling, simulation, systematic trial and error). At least 80% of the activities/costs of the business component must be experimental; if the overall pilot model fails, the taxpayer must provide granular cost records isolating the specific sub-component that meets the 80% test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).

Taxpayer Failure: Selling the mold to the customer (the fact pattern that avoided the depreciation exclusion in TG Missouri) under a cost-plus or guaranteed progress-payment contract, or signing OEM standard terms that assign all underlying IP, CAD designs, and technical know-how exclusively to the customer.

Dual Contingency & IP Retention Standard: Within the four corners of the customer contract, payment for the resold mold must be contingent on technical success (e.g., fixed-price payment conditioned on passing PPAP/acceptance trials), and the taxpayer must retain substantial, non-incidental rights to use the underlying engineering designs and manufacturing know-how in future projects without paying royalties.

Taxpayer Failure: Retrospectively estimating supply allocations or employee engineering hours through oral testimony without job-order cost accounting linking specific vendor invoices and trial runs to discrete business components.

Direct Accounting Nexus Standard: Supply and wage QREs must be linked directly to qualified research activities and discrete business components via the taxpayer's contemporaneous accounting system (job summary reports, WBS codes, general ledger sub-accounts, and trial logs), leaving minimal reliance on Cohan estimation.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how corporate taxpayers in the United States can operationalize the holding of TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner while insulating their claims against the post-TG Missouri litigation pitfalls identified in Union Carbide, Little Sandy Coal, Tangel, Phoenix Design Group, and System Technologies, the following two applied industry case studies provide step-by-step remedial blueprints.
Case Study 1: Tier-1 Automotive Precision Injection-Molding & Structural Composite Supplier (Multi-Cavity Tooling Resold to OEM Customers)
Project Scenario and Initial Legal Pitfalls

Apex Polymer Systems, Inc. ("Apex"), a United States Tier-1 automotive supplier based in Missouri, receives an RFQ from a major domestic automotive OEM to design and manufacture an ultra-lightweight, structural glass-fiber-reinforced thermoplastic battery housing tray for a new electric vehicle (EV) platform. To meet stringent crash-worthiness, electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding, and dimensional flatness tolerances ( across a span), Apex must design a novel 2,500-ton high-pressure compression-injection production mold featuring a proprietary multi-zone sequential valve-gate hot-runner system and 3D-printed conformal cooling channels.

Apex's engineers spend 4,200 hours designing the mold geometry, and Apex pays $1.4 million to a third-party precision toolmaker ("Midwest Tool & Die") to machine and assemble the steel mold, plus $180,000 for specialized long-glass-fiber polypropylene resin used during T0, T1, and T2 mold trial runs. Upon completion of the trials, Apex sells the mold to the OEM for $1.65 million, retains physical custody of the mold at its plant to produce commercial battery trays, and claims the $1.4 million toolmaker cost and $180,000 resin cost as supply QREs under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).

Under current IRS examination guidelines, Apex's claim faces four disqualifying defects. First, regarding accounting and depreciation under TG Missouri, Apex booked the $1.4 million paid to Midwest Tool & Die into a general "Capital Tooling & Equipment" ledger account that commingles self-retained maintenance fixtures with customer-billed molds, and inadvertently claimed MACRS depreciation on a portion of the sub-account on Form 4562. Second, regarding third-party vendor risk under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3) and (b)(5), Apex's standard purchase order to Midwest Tool & Die states that the vendor warrants the finished mold will produce parts meeting OEM print tolerances and makes the final 30 percent payment contingent on successful OEM PPAP sign-off, thereby shifting the technical risk of mold success to the third-party toolmaker. Third, regarding the funded research exclusion under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), the OEM's standard Tooling Purchase Order contains a "Work Made for Hire / Exclusive Property" clause vesting 100 percent of all rights, title, and interest in the mold and all underlying CAD designs, gating calculations, and tooling concepts in the OEM, while reimbursing Apex on a non-refundable milestone basis at 30 percent upon kickoff, 40 percent upon steel cut, and 30 percent upon delivery. Fourth, regarding inventory commingling under Union Carbide, the $180,000 of trial resin was requisitioned from Apex's general commercial raw material silo, and 15 percent of the molded battery trays from the T2 trial run were later sold to the OEM as commercial service parts without cost segregation.
Step 1: Project Governance and Fixed-Asset / WIP Accounting Segregation

To satisfy the "in the hands of the taxpayer" non-depreciability standard of TG Missouri, Apex's tax and corporate accounting departments must establish strict general ledger isolation prior to project inception. Specifically, Apex must create a dedicated non-capital general ledger account titled Account 1350 (Customer-Resold Experimental Tooling – Non-Depreciable WIP) that is structurally blocked in the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system from feeding into the fixed-asset sub-ledger or Form 4562 depreciation schedules. All third-party toolmaker invoices for molds destined for customer resale must be coded exclusively to Account 1350, whereas internal shop fixtures or backup molds owned and retained by Apex must be routed to Account 1700 (Capital Machinery & Equipment) and excluded from supply QREs.

Simultaneously, to prepare for a potential IRS challenge under the 80 percent "substantially all" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), Apex must structure the ERP project code (PRJ-EV-2026-04) into discrete Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) child nodes corresponding to functional sub-assemblies of the mold. If an IRS engineer argues that the standard mold base exceeds 20 percent of total mold cost and causes the overall mold assembly to fail the 80 percent test, Apex can immediately invoke the shrink-back rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and claim 100 percent of the vendor invoices and labor mapped to the experimental sub-assemblies, as detailed in the table below.

Standard Outer Mold Base & Ejector Housing
Carved Out Under Shrink-Back: Excluded if the total mold fails the macro 80% test, preserving $1,120,000 in WBS-04.1 through 04.3.
Qualified Supply QRE: Excludes $27,000 (15%) of T2 parts sold commercially, satisfying Union Carbide.

body.text: Step 2: Contractual Restructuring of Customer and Vendor Agreements

Apex's legal counsel must execute two bilateral contractual modifications before incurring tooling expenses to harmonize TG Missouri with the funded research and vendor risk rules. In restructuring the OEM Customer Tooling Contract to satisfy TG Missouri, Populous Holdings, and System Technologies, Apex must first establish an explicit transfer of legal title coupled with a bailment for production. The Tooling Agreement must state that legal title and ownership of the physical production mold transfers to the OEM upon successful completion of the Production Part Approval Process (PPAP) and issuance of a signed Part Submission Warrant (PSW), after which Apex holds the physical mold solely as a bailee at will. To mirror the facts the Court relied on in TG Missouri, the agreement should also place the risk of loss for the mold on the OEM and price the mold separately rather than through higher per-unit part prices, supporting the position that Apex has no economic interest in the mold and that it is not depreciable property in Apex's hands under I.R.C. §§ 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and 174(c).

Within that same OEM agreement, Apex must eliminate non-refundable progress payments and stipulate that the contract is a firm fixed-price agreement where 100 percent of the OEM's payment obligation is contingent upon the mold successfully producing parts that pass rigorous dimensional, structural-load, and thermal-cycling validation under PPAP. An explicit clawback clause must require Apex to refund any interim financing advances at its own expense if the mold design fails to achieve PPAP approval. Furthermore, to satisfy the substantial rights prong under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the contract must include an intellectual property bifurcation clause: while the OEM receives legal title to the physical steel mold and exclusive rights to the exact part-surface geometry of its proprietary battery tray, Apex retains full ownership and perpetual, royalty-free, non-exclusive substantial rights to all underlying mold engineering designs, sequential gating algorithms, conformal cooling methodologies, and manufacturing know-how developed during the project.

Concurrently, in restructuring the Third-Party Toolmaker Purchase Order to satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3) and (b)(5), Example 1, Apex must remove any turnkey design performance warranty from the purchase order issued to Midwest Tool & Die. The Toolmaker Purchase Order must specify that Apex provides the complete 3D CAD mold design, gating specifications, and tool-path prints, and orders Midwest Tool & Die to fabricate the mold components strictly "upon Apex's order and at Apex's design risk". Under this revised structure, Midwest Tool & Die warrants only that the machined steel conforms to Apex's blueprints and metallurgical specifications (a standard workmanship warranty), while Apex bears 100 percent of the financial cost of re-machining, welding, or scrapping inserts if Apex's mold design fails to fill properly or warps during injection trials.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Uncertainty at Project Outset

To preempt a Phoenix Design Group challenge, Apex's lead tooling engineer must author a contemporaneous Pre-Design Technical Uncertainty Charter at the RFQ award stage, documenting specific method and design uncertainties prior to CAD modeling. This charter must detail why existing injection-molding engineering standards and empirical data available to Apex cannot predict fiber-orientation anisotropy, weld-line structural weakness, and differential shrinkage across a thin-wall long-glass-fiber composite tray. It must also establish competing engineering hypotheses regarding gate locations (comparing an 8-drop versus a 12-drop sequential cascade configuration), runner diameters, and conformal cooling channel proximity required to prevent warpage exceeding the flatness specification.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Trial Material Isolation

During execution, Apex must maintain chronological Moldflow finite element analysis (FEA) simulation iterations linked directly to physical T0, T1, and T2 press try-out sheets, Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) laser-scan reports showing out-of-spec warpage, and Engineering Change Notices (ECNs) documenting steel-safe modifications ordered from Midwest Tool & Die between trials. To overcome Union Carbide, Apex must purchase the trial-run resin under a dedicated R&D purchase order stored in a quarantined engineering bin rather than drawing from commercial Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) inventory. Prototype battery trays molded during T0 through T2 trials must be subjected to destructive mechanical testing or scrapped with signed scrap certificates; for the 15 percent of T2 validation parts ($27,000 of resin) that are ultimately sold to the OEM as service parts, their proportional raw material cost must be credited back out of the R&D supply account and transferred to commercial COGS, leaving only the $153,000 of purely experimental consumed resin in the QRE calculation.
Case Study 2: Custom Industrial Air-Flow & Volatile Organic Compound (VOC) Abatement Systems Manufacturer (First-in-Class Commercial Pilot Models Delivered to Customers)
Project Scenario and Initial Legal Pitfalls

AeroPure Environmental Corp. ("AeroPure"), a specialty industrial equipment manufacturer in the United States, designs and builds custom industrial air-flow and thermal oxidizer emission-control systems for semiconductor and pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities—a factual profile directly analogous to Stephens v. Commissioner (involving custom air-flow systems built by CESI and QASI). AeroPure enters into a $5.5 million contract with a specialty chemical manufacturer ("ChemCo") to design, fabricate, and deliver a custom high-volume Regenerative Catalytic Oxidizer (RCO) and variable-vortex air-flow handling system capable of destroying 99.8 percent of halogenated VOCs at 40 percent lower thermal energy consumption than any system AeroPure has previously built.

Because each system is custom-engineered and fabricated as a single unit delivered directly to the customer's plant, AeroPure builds the entire system—incurring $3.2 million in specialized hastelloy sheet metal, ceramic honeycomb catalyst beds, high-temperature dampers, structural steel housing, and commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) exhaust fans purchased from third-party vendors—tests the integrated system during factory and site commissioning, transfers title to ChemCo, and claims the entire $3.2 million material cost as a "pilot model" supply QRE under TG Missouri, Stephens, and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4).

AeroPure's $3.2 million supply claim is highly vulnerable to complete disallowance on four grounds. First, regarding failure of the 80 percent "substantially all" test and lack of shrink-back records under Little Sandy Coal and Betz, while the novel dual-bed catalytic reactor core and the high-speed rotary vortex switching valve required extensive fluid-dynamic experimentation, 42 percent of the $3.2 million material cost consisted of structural support frames, external insulation cladding, standard COTS exhaust blower motors, and straight sheet-metal ductwork that involved zero technological uncertainty. Because AeroPure tracked all $3.2 million of materials in a single job-cost bucket (Job #4092), the entire system fails the 80 percent "substantially all" process of experimentation test, and AeroPure lacks the sub-component accounting needed to apply the shrink-back rule. Second, under Stephens and Little Sandy Coal, the IRS will argue that the air-flow system is not an investigative "pilot model" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) because it was built to fulfill a commercial delivery contract rather than solely to develop the concept of a product. Third, regarding depreciation versus sale timing ambiguity under TG Missouri, because the project spanned two tax years (2025 and 2026) and AeroPure retained title during factory testing in late 2025 while listing the partially completed unit under "Construction in Progress (CIP) – Plant Assets" on its balance sheet, the IRS will contend the asset was depreciable property in AeroPure's hands. Fourth, under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A), AeroPure improperly included supply replacements and technician wages incurred during routine customer operator training and post-acceptance warranty adjustments after the system had already passed performance validation and entered commercial operation at ChemCo's facility.
Step 1: Project Governance and "Shrink-Back" Sub-Component Cost Architecture

To prevent the non-experimental structural steel, standard ductwork, and COTS blower motors from contaminating the experimental subsystems under Little Sandy Coal and Trinity Industries, AeroPure must restructure its project accounting before fabrication begins. Rather than defining the entire $5.5 million delivered air-flow facility as a single monolithic business component, AeroPure's engineering governance committee must formally designate discrete functional sub-assemblies as independent business components in the ERP job-cost system pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Every purchase requisition, bill of materials (BOM) item, and third-party vendor invoice must carry a mandatory WBS sub-component tag, isolating the experimental pilot model subsystems from the balance of plant as shown in the table below.

body.text: By voluntarily excluding BC-4092-C ($1.33 million) and claiming only the $1.87 million of supplies directly mapped to BC-4092-A and BC-4092-B, AeroPure satisfies the 80 percent "substantially all" rule on each claimed sub-component with mathematical precision.
Step 2: Contractual Restructuring for Pilot Model Resale and Economic Risk

To leverage TG Missouri and Stephens simultaneously, AeroPure must structure its customer contract with ChemCo to prove that the delivered sub-assemblies are non-depreciable pilot models constructed at AeroPure's technical and financial risk. First, to establish non-depreciable resale characterization under TG Missouri, the contract must explicitly classify the system as custom-fabricated equipment produced for sale to ChemCo, and AeroPure's accounting department must record all fabrication costs across 2025 and 2026 in Customer Contract WIP – Goods Held for Sale rather than Construction in Progress (CIP) – Capital Assets. Under TG Missouri, because AeroPure holds the equipment solely for resale to ChemCo and never places it into service for AeroPure's own depreciable use under I.R.C. § 167, and AeroPure retains no economic interest in the equipment after its sale (for example, because ChemCo bears the risk of loss once title passes), the supplies used to construct the subsystems should fall outside the depreciable property exclusion of I.R.C. §§ 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and 174(c).

Second, to satisfy Stephens and System Technologies, AeroPure must incorporate a "First-of-Kind Engineering Development & Performance Acceptance" schedule into the ChemCo contract. This schedule must explicitly state that achieving the 99.8 percent halogenated VOC destruction efficiency and 40 percent thermal recovery target requires experimental design and full-scale physical pilot-model validation of the catalytic core (BC-4092-A) and rotary vortex damper (BC-4092-B) because small-scale bench testing cannot replicate turbulent multi-phase gas flow. Furthermore, the contract must mandate that final acceptance and payment of the fixed contract price are strictly contingent upon the delivered system passing a continuous 72-hour EPA Method 25A emissions and thermal efficiency validation test; if the system fails to meet the guaranteed parameters, AeroPure is contractually obligated to re-engineer and rebuild the core and damper assemblies at its sole expense or remove the equipment and refund all prior milestone payments. Finally, the contract must confirm that AeroPure retains all intellectual property rights, patent rights, and engineering designs for the catalytic core and rotary damper technology.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Design Uncertainty

To establish that the fabricated sub-assemblies satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) and (a)(4) as investigative pilot models rather than routine custom builds, AeroPure's engineering team must compile a Baseline Engineering Uncertainty Dossier prior to metal fabrication. This dossier must contain thermodynamic and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) calculations demonstrating why existing damper seal geometries warp under acid-gas thermal shock and why standard catalyst bed depths suffer flow channeling and pressure-drop spikes above. Crucially, the dossier must document why a full-scale functional representation (pilot model) is the only engineering method capable of testing the fluid-dynamic interaction between the rotary vortex damper switching frequency and pressure surges across the ceramic catalyst bed.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Commercial Production Cut-Off Controls

Throughout the design and testing lifecycle, AeroPure must require all mechanical, chemical, and controls engineers to log daily hours in AeroPure's time-tracking system directly against sub-components BC-4092-A and BC-4092-B, paired with mandatory technical activity narratives (such as CFD modeling, prototype fabrication supervision, factory flow-loop testing, and catalyst bed modification) rather than generic project administration codes. AeroPure must retain all empirical test logs showing failed seal pressure tests during Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT), subsequent redesign of the hastelloy labyrinth seal, and re-testing results. Finally, to enforce a hard cut-off at the onset of commercial production under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A), AeroPure must implement an automated ERP accounting gate triggered the moment the 72-hour site emissions validation test succeeds and ChemCo signs the Certificate of Technical Acceptance, immediately locking BC-4092-A and BC-4092-B against any further R&D charges so that subsequent customer training, routine commissioning adjustments, and warranty maintenance are routed exclusively to non-qualifying post-production cost centers.
5. Strategic Synthesis and Compliance Conclusions

The United States Tax Court's decision in TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), remains a leading authority on whether customer-sold production molds (and, by extension, other customer-sold tooling and pilot models) can qualify as supply QREs under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). By rejecting the IRS's generic "inherent physical character" test and establishing that the depreciable property exclusion of I.R.C. §§ 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and 174(c) applies only when property is depreciable in the hands of the taxpayer, the Court confirmed that manufacturers who sell experimental tooling or custom pilot models to customers and retain no economic interest in them—even if they keep physical possession to produce parts—are not barred from claiming third-party fabrication and material costs as qualified supplies.

However, as subsequent federal jurisprudence in Union Carbide, Trinity Industries, Little Sandy Coal, Stephens, Tangel, Phoenix Design Group, and System Technologies demonstrates, TG Missouri is a necessary threshold victory rather than a standalone safe harbor. Because the depreciation exclusion is avoided only where the property is not depreciable in the taxpayer's hands (as when the taxpayer sells the production mold or pilot model to a customer and retains no economic interest in it, as in TG Missouri), corporate taxpayers must simultaneously engineer their commercial contracts and accounting systems to navigate four intersecting statutory requirements: segregating customer-resold tooling from self-retained depreciable capital assets on the general ledger; ensuring third-party toolmaker purchase orders place design control and technical failure risk squarely on the taxpayer pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(3) and (b)(5), Example 1; structuring customer resale contracts with strict technical acceptance contingencies and IP retention clauses to defeat the funded research exclusion under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); and implementing granular WBS sub-component cost accounting to satisfy the 80 percent "substantially all" process of experimentation requirement via the shrink-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). When these legal, contractual, and accounting controls are integrated prospectively, United States manufacturers can sustain substantial supply and pilot-model R&D tax credit claims upon IRS examination and judicial review.
